chapter: Chapter II - Right to Information and Obligations of Public Authorities
text: Section 7(1): Disposal of request. A Public Information Officer must decide on an information request and provide the information within thirty days of receiving the request. Where the information concerns the life or liberty of a person, it must be provided within forty-eight hours. If the request is refused, the PIO must give reasons and the name and designation of the officer responsible.

Section 19(1) and 19(3): Appeals. A person who does not receive a decision within the time limit, or who is aggrieved by a decision, may file a first appeal to an officer senior to the PIO within thirty days. A second appeal may then be made to the State or Central Information Commission within ninety days of the first appellate decision or its due date.

act: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
chapter: Chapter IV - Procedure for Obtaining Orders of Reliefs
text: Section 12: Application to Magistrate. An aggrieved woman, or any person on her behalf, may present an application to the Magistrate seeking one or more reliefs under this Act. The Magistrate may pass orders including protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, custody orders, and compensation for injuries or mental distress. The aggrieved person may also approach a Protection Officer or a service provider, and no fee is payable for filing.

chapter: Chapter V - Leases of Immoveable Property
text: Section 106: Duration of certain leases in absence of written contract. Where no written lease exists, a lease for agricultural or manufacturing purposes is deemed to be from year to year. A lease for any other purpose, such as residential or commercial tenancy, is deemed to be month to month. A month-to-month tenancy may be terminated by either party by fifteen days' notice expiring with the end of a month. Parties may agree to different terms in a written contract.

chapter: Chapter VI - Consequences of Breach of Contract
text: Section 74: Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated. When a contract names a sum payable on breach, or contains a penalty clause, the injured party may recover only reasonable compensation not exceeding the named amount. Courts may award reasonable compensation even where actual loss cannot be proved. This limits excessive penalty clauses in agreements.

Section 303: Theft. Whoever dishonestly moves any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, with the intention of taking it, commits theft. The offence is punishable with imprisonment up to three years, or fine, or both, for a first conviction. This section replaced Section 378 and 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, from 1 July 2024.

Section 318: Cheating. Whoever deceives any person, fraudulently or dishonestly inducing that person to deliver property or to consent to retention of property, or to do or omit something he would not otherwise do, commits cheating. Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property is punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine. This section replaced Sections 415 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, from 1 July 2024.

Article 21: Protection of life and personal liberty. No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. The Supreme Court has interpreted this right to include the right to live with human dignity, the right to privacy, and the right to a speedy trial.

chapter: Part III and Part V - Remedies for Enforcement of Rights
text: Articles 32 and 226: Right to constitutional remedies. Article 32 allows any person to approach the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Article 226 allows High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose. These are the constitutional routes for seeking relief when a fundamental right is violated.
